name: Battle of the Bulge
info: A German offensive through the Ardennes in Belgium and Luxembourg took the Western Allies by surprise on 16 December 1944 but was halted short of the Meuse, and the front was restored by the end of January 1945.

facts.place: The Ardennes region of eastern Belgium and northern Luxembourg, with fighting at Elsenborn Ridge, St. Vith and Bastogne
facts.sides: Germany under Hitler, with Army Group B under Walter Model and OB West under Gerd von Rundstedt, who committed over 410,000 men, just over 1,400 tanks and armoured fighting vehicles, 2,600 artillery pieces and over 1,000 combat aircraft; the western Allies under Dwight D. Eisenhower, whose forces eventually numbered more than 700,000 men
facts.outcome: The German offensive was halted short of the Meuse and broken by 27 December, and the front line was effectively restored to its pre-attack position by the end of January. Casualties are put at between 63,000 and 104,000 for the Germans and 77,000 to more than 83,000 for the Allies.

t: The Germans achieved total surprise on 16 December 1944 through Allied overconfidence, faulty intelligence, poor aerial reconnaissance in bad weather and a preoccupation with Allied offensive plans elsewhere.
American resistance around Elsenborn Ridge in the north and Bastogne in the south blocked key roads, and the congestion and defender-friendly terrain put the German advance behind schedule.
The battle severely depleted Germany's armoured forces, which remained largely unreplaced for the rest of the war, and it was the last major offensive the Axis powers attempted on the Western Front.
dyk: When German infiltrators in American uniforms caused alarm behind the Allied lines, military policemen quizzed troops on things every American was expected to know, and General Omar Bradley was briefly detained after he correctly named Springfield as the capital of Illinois, because the policeman believed it was Chicago.
ev: Hitler first outlines a counter-offensive to his generals on 16 September
On 16 December the Germans open the offensive with a 90-minute barrage and achieve total surprise
On 17 December prisoners are shot near Baugnez in the Malmedy massacre
On 19 December the 101st Airborne Division reaches Bastogne by truck, and the town is cut off on 20 December
On 24 December the furthest German advance is stopped at Foy-Notre-Dame by the U.S. 2nd Armored Division
On 26 December the lead element of Patton's Third Army reaches Bastogne from the south and ends the siege
On 16 January the U.S. First and Third Armies link up at Houffalize
The offensive closes on 25 January, though the last German units do not return to their start line until February

sections.background:
After the breakout from Normandy at the end of July 1944 and the Allied landings in southern France on 15 August 1944, the Allies advanced towards Germany more quickly than anticipated. Troops were fatigued, supply lines were stretched extremely thin and supplies were dangerously depleted. The Allies captured Antwerp intact in the first days of September, but it was not operational until 28 November, because the Schelde estuary had to be cleared of German troops and naval mines. Eisenhower and Field Marshal Montgomery differed over whether Montgomery or Lieutenant General Omar Bradley would get priority access to supplies, and Eisenhower preferred a broad-front strategy.

The German situation remained dire. There were 96 Allied divisions at or near the front, and the Germans could field a total of 55 understrength divisions. Hitler first outlined his counter-offensive to his generals on 16 September 1944. He believed that a blow in the west would split the Allied forces and compel the Americans and British to settle for a separate peace. After the war this assessment was generally viewed as unrealistic, given Allied air superiority.

By December Eisenhower and his staff had decided to hold the Ardennes primarily as a rest area for the U.S. First Army. The line there was thinly held, because of the favourable defensive terrain and because the Allies had intelligence that the Wehrmacht was using the area across the German border as a rest-and-refit area.
sections.forces:
The Germans committed over 410,000 men, just over 1,400 tanks and armoured fighting vehicles, 2,600 artillery pieces and over 1,000 combat aircraft. Allied forces eventually numbered more than 700,000 men. Field Marshal Walter Model's Army Group B and Field Marshal Gerd von Rundstedt, commanding OB West, were put in charge of the operation. The 6th Panzer Army under Sepp Dietrich had the lead role and the shortest route to Antwerp; the Fifth Panzer Army under Hasso von Manteuffel was to take Brussels; and the Seventh Army under Erich Brandenberger, with four infantry divisions, was to protect the southern flank.

The plan originally called for just under 45 divisions, but a manpower shortage reduced the force to around 30. Among them were Volksgrenadier units formed from veterans and from recruits formerly regarded as too young, too old or too frail to fight. Four conditions were thought critical: complete surprise, poor weather to neutralise Allied air power, a rapid advance to the Meuse by day four, and the capture of Allied fuel, since the General Staff estimated that its fuel covered only one third to one half of the ground to Antwerp. Model and von Rundstedt thought Antwerp too ambitious and proposed a smaller plan, but Hitler would not listen. Operation Greif, in which English-speaking Germans in American and British uniforms were to disrupt the rear, was added.

The U.S. units in the Ardennes were a mixture of inexperienced troops, such as the 99th and 106th Divisions, and battle-hardened troops sent to recuperate, such as the 28th Infantry Division.
sections.course:
At 05:30 on 16 December 1944 the Germans began a 90-minute barrage by 1,600 artillery pieces across a front of 130 kilometres. Heavy snowstorms kept Allied aircraft grounded but also hampered the German advance, and poor traffic control led to traffic jams and fuel shortages in forward units. In the north, the U.S. 2nd and 99th Infantry Divisions held Elsenborn Ridge and forced the German spearhead onto less favourable routes further south. Kampfgruppe Peiper, of 4,800 men and 600 vehicles, was more than 16 hours behind schedule; on 17 December SS troops shot prisoners near Baugnez, and at least 84 American prisoners were murdered. Peiper reached Stavelot and La Gleize but found bridges blown and fuel short.

In the centre, the Fifth Panzer Army surrounded two regiments of the 106th Division on the Schnee Eifel and forced their surrender. The defenders of St. Vith, led by the 7th Armored Division, slowed the advance until the town was evacuated on 21 December. In the south, the 101st Airborne Division reached Bastogne by truck on 19 December, and the Germans surrounded the town on 20 December. When the German commander asked for its surrender, Brigadier General Anthony McAuliffe replied "NUTS!".

The weather began to clear on 23 December, allowing Allied air attacks. On 24 December the furthest German advance, at Foy-Notre-Dame, was stopped. On 26 December Company D, 37th Tank Battalion of the 4th Armored Division reached Bastogne at 16:50, ending the siege.
sections.aftermath:
Montgomery launched his attack from the north on 3 January 1945, two days after the date Eisenhower wanted, and Patton's Third Army fought from the south. On 7 and 8 January Hitler agreed to withdraw gradually from the tip of the salient. The First and Third Armies linked up at Houffalize on 16 January, the Americans recaptured St. Vith on 23 January, and the last German units did not return to their start line until February. On 1 January the Luftwaffe attacked Allied airfields in Operation Bodenplatte, destroying or severely damaging some 465 aircraft and losing 277 planes, and Operation Nordwind began against the U.S. Seventh Army in Alsace, closing on 25 January.

Counts of the casualties differ. German losses are put at between 63,000 and 104,000 killed, missing, wounded or captured, and Allied casualties at 77,000 to more than 83,000, including at least 8,600 killed. American soldiers killed about sixty German prisoners near Chenogne on 1 January, and eleven black American soldiers were tortured and shot at Wereth on 17 December; the perpetrators were never punished.

The German offensive inflicted heavy losses and set back the Allied invasion of Germany by several weeks, but the Germans' last reserves were gone and the Luftwaffe was shattered. On 12 January the Red Army began the Vistula–Oder offensive, brought forward from 20 January.
sections.sources:
Much of the Allied side of the story rests on intelligence records. At Bletchley Park, F. L. Lucas and Peter Calvocoressi of Hut 3 wrote a report on the handling of Ultra before the battle, concluding that the intelligence was plentiful but misread and misused. A report by the Chief of the Secret Intelligence Service, issued on 28 December 1944, drew similar lessons and stressed over-reliance on Ultra and poor Allied security. The U.S. Army's official history is the source for the loss of at least 7,000 men on the Schnee Eifel, probably 8,000 or 9,000.

Several accounts are disputed or come second hand. Accounts of the Malmedy killing vary, and Peiper, Dietrich and others were tried for it. Dietrich's postwar story about his plan to cross the Meuse shifted under questioning. Manteuffel's praise of Montgomery comes from interviews by B. H. Liddell Hart, who has been accused of putting words in the mouths of German generals. Casualty totals vary with the source: the German High Command accepted 81,834 for its own losses, while the U.S. Army Center of Military History gives 100,000 German and 75,000 American casualties.

Historians also disagree over weight. John S. D. Eisenhower called the action of the 2nd and 99th Divisions on the northern shoulder possibly the most decisive of the campaign. Stephen Ambrose wrote in 1997 that putting Montgomery in command in the north had no effect on the battle, while John Buckley wrote in 2013 that Montgomery must take considerable credit for stabilising it. There were no correspondents around St. Vith, Elsenborn or Monschau-Höfen.
sections.legacy:
The Battle of the Bulge was the largest and bloodiest single battle fought by the United States in the Second World War, and it marked the last major offensive attempted by the Axis powers on the Western Front. Its names reflect different views: the Germans used Unternehmen Wacht am Rhein, the Allies called it the Ardennes Counteroffensive, and the press coined "Bulge" from the shape of the front on news maps. Winston Churchill told the House of Commons that it was undoubtedly the greatest American battle of the war and would, he believed, be regarded as an ever-famous American victory.

The battle left a quarrel behind. At a press conference on 7 January, Montgomery gave the impression, in the ears of American leaders, that he had taken the lion's share of the credit. Bradley and Patton threatened to resign unless his command was changed, and Eisenhower decided to dismiss him before the chiefs of staff, de Guingand and Walter Smith, moved him to reconsider. Montgomery later wrote that he should never have held the conference.

Because of troop shortages, Eisenhower decided to integrate the service for the first time during the battle, with more than 2,000 black soldiers volunteering to go to the front, an important step towards a desegregated U.S. military. After the war the U.S. Army issued the Ardennes-Alsace campaign citation to units that took part. Bastogne, with its resupply by parachute and glider and Patton's fast response, captured the public's imagination in the press.

summary: The Ardennes Offensive began on 16 December 1944 with a surprise German attack on thinly held American lines. It was halted short of the Meuse by the end of December, and the front was restored by the end of January 1945. Casualties on each side ran to tens of thousands.
references: Antony Beevor, Ardennes 1944: Hitler's Last Gamble (Viking, 2015)
Peter Caddick-Adams, Snow and Steel: The Battle of the Bulge, 1944–45 (Oxford University Press, 2015)
Hugh M. Cole, The Ardennes: Battle of the Bulge (Office of the Chief of Military History Department of the Army, 1964)
John S.D. Eisenhower, The Bitter Woods (G.P. Putnam's Sons, 1969)
Trevor N. Dupuy, Hitler's Last Gamble: The Battle of the Bulge, December 1944 – January 1945 (HarperCollins, 1994)
Christer Bergström, The Ardennes: Hitler's Winter Offensive 1944–1945 (Casemate Publishers, 2014)
notes: The article names Elsenborn Ridge as 'the decisive component' and later quotes John S. D. Eisenhower on the northern shoulder; I give only the quotation, attributed.

Left out as garbled or inconsistent: a final attack by the 246th Volksgrenadier Division 'on 26 February' against Elsenborn Ridge (the date does not fit the battle); 'Pieper' for Peiper; 'Eiffel sector'; an unnamed 'Robertson' who had decided to abandon the villages; the 'as high as 125,000' German casualty estimate, which is followed by an empty quotation.
Peiper's force: 4,800 men and 600 vehicles; of this, about 800 escaped on 23 December. Not given in the text for length.

The article says 'The Siege of Bastogne had lasted barely a week' and gives 21 December as the date it was surrounded in one place and 20 December in another; I wrote 20 December for the cutting off of the town (course) and kept 'surrounded' loosely.

Allied casualty figures are many: preliminary First and Third Armies report 75,482 (8,407 killed); MacDonald 81,000; Army report 105,102 for the whole Ardennes-Alsace campaign; Dupuy 62,439 for divisions. I give the lead's range and the Center of Military History's figures only. German figures likewise: High Command 81,834 (12,652 killed), Dupuy 74,459 for divisions, Jung 67,675.

Left out: Malmedy trial detail, Wereth detail beyond what is given, Skorzeny's trial, tank loss figures, the unit lists of the initial assault (empty in the article), the long Montgomery quotations, Patton's remarks at Verdun, the Cine Rex V-2 strike, the Ultra indicators list.
The Malmedy figure is the article's 'at least 84' (accounts vary). The Wereth killing is the article's 'Wereth 11'.
Left out of ev: Antwerp operational on 28 November and the delay of the start from 27 November to 16 December.
